editorial.headline: Guarantee Agency Activity: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: An agency role marketing guarantee-business activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet PMA registration at a Bali address is blocked by the island-wide moratorium.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor seeking a Bali address, this activity cannot be registered today. That is the decisive local fact, even though its national record is open. KBLI 66224 covers agency activity in the guarantee sector: marketing the business activities of guarantee companies or sharia guarantee companies, for and on their behalf. It is a defined representative and market-facing role, not a catch-all description of commercial activity. The scope stays anchored to both the marketing function and the named guarantee businesses whose activity is being marketed. It does not merely name an industry; it specifies marketing undertaken for and on behalf of those businesses.

Nationally, the position is clear. The code is TERBUKA and sets a maximum foreign ownership of 100%, which permits full foreign ownership at the national level. It is available at each listed scale—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. The range of scales widens the set of possible registrations, but does not widen the scope: at any of those scales, the activity recorded here remains the marketing of guarantee-business activity for and on behalf of a guarantee company or sharia guarantee company. Scale is a registration attribute, not a substitute for the stated marketing mandate.

Bali produces a different answer for PMA registration. The Bali record is CHIUSO_MORATORIA_BALI and expressly flags the activity as blocked. Its stated reason places the Besar scale in the Menengah Rendah category for this purpose. Bali’s rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis. A national ceiling of 100% therefore does not create a route to a Bali address: for a foreign investor, the moratorium controls the registration outcome there.

This is not a marginal caveat to be addressed after the national analysis; it is the practical dividing line. The national entry describes an activity that is open to foreign ownership, while Bali’s rule bars a PMA registration for the same activity at a Bali address. Founders should read both statements together, beginning with the real activity—marketing undertaken for the named guarantee businesses—and then the listed scale. Only then does the apparent contradiction resolve: national openness and a Bali registration block can coexist.
